langchain: In LangChain Expression Language (LCEL), what does the | operator do in chain = prompt | model | parser?
Composes runnables so each output feeds the next input
Runs all three runnables in parallel on the same input
Tries each runnable in turn until one succeeds
Merges the outputs of all three into one dictionary
The pipe operator builds a RunnableSequence: the prompt output goes to the model, and the model output goes to the parser.
Which method do you call to run a LangChain runnable once on a single input and get the final result?
invoke()
batch()
stream()
transform()
invoke() runs the runnable on one input and returns the full output. batch() takes a list of inputs and stream() yields chunks.
In the LCEL chain {"context": retriever, "question": RunnablePassthrough()} | prompt, what does RunnablePassthrough() supply?
The original chain input, unchanged, as question
An empty string whenever the retriever finds nothing
The retriever output copied into the question key
The previous turn of the conversation from memory
RunnablePassthrough returns its input as is, so the user question flows to the prompt next to the retrieved context.
When a plain dict such as {"a": chain1, "b": chain2} is used as a step in an LCEL chain, which runnable does LangChain turn it into?
RunnableParallel
RunnableSequence
RunnableBranch
RunnableLambda
A dict of runnables is coerced into RunnableParallel, which runs each value on the same input and returns a dict of results.
Which class explicitly wraps an ordinary Python function so it becomes a LangChain runnable with invoke, batch and stream?
RunnableLambda
RunnablePassthrough
RunnableParallel
RunnableBinding
RunnableLambda(func) turns any callable into a runnable. RunnablePassthrough forwards input and does not wrap custom logic.
What does PromptTemplate.from_template("Tell me a joke about {topic}").invoke({"topic": "cats"}) return?
A prompt value whose text is the filled-in template
A model response that contains a joke about cats
The template string with {topic} left unchanged
A list with one HumanMessage per template variable
A prompt template only formats text; invoking it returns a StringPromptValue. No model is called until you pipe it into one.
Which element lets a ChatPromptTemplate insert a variable-length list of earlier chat messages, for example chat history?
MessagesPlaceholder
FewShotPromptTemplate
SystemMessagePromptTemplate
StringPromptValue
MessagesPlaceholder("history") reserves a slot that is filled with a list of messages at invoke time.
A prompt is ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([("system", "You are a {role}"), ("human", "{question}")]). Which input keys must invoke receive?
role and question
Only question
system and human
messages and question
Every {variable} in any message of the template is an input variable, including the one inside the system message.
What does StrOutputParser do when it receives an AIMessage from a chat model in an LCEL chain?
Returns the message content as a plain string
Splits the content into a list of separate lines
Parses the content as JSON and returns a dict
Wraps the content in a new HumanMessage object
StrOutputParser extracts the text content, which is why prompt | model | StrOutputParser() returns a str.
With PydanticOutputParser, which method returns text you put in the prompt so the model knows the expected output format?
get_format_instructions()
get_output_schema_text()
format_prompt_hint()
to_prompt_instructions()
get_format_instructions() describes the JSON schema derived from the Pydantic model; you usually inject it as a prompt variable.
For a chat model that supports tool calling or JSON output, what is the recommended LangChain way to get results as instances of a Pydantic class?
model.with_structured_output(MyModel)
model.bind_parser(MyModel)
model.as_pydantic(MyModel)
model.with_output_schema(MyModel)
with_structured_output uses the provider's native structured output features and returns parsed objects of the given schema.
You call stream() on prompt | model | JsonOutputParser(). What does the stream yield?
Increasingly complete partial JSON objects
Nothing until the whole output is valid JSON
Single raw string tokens from the model
A JSON schema that describes the output
JsonOutputParser supports streaming: it parses the partial text so far and yields progressively more complete objects.
What does calling load() on a typical LangChain document loader return?
A list of Document objects with page_content and metadata
One string that contains the text of every file
A vector store already filled with embeddings
A dict that maps each file name to its raw bytes
Loaders return Document objects. Splitting, embedding and indexing are separate steps.
You must process millions of files with a LangChain loader without holding every Document in memory. Which loader method fits?
lazy_load()
load()
load_and_split()
aload()
lazy_load() is a generator that yields Documents one at a time. load() and aload() return the full list at once.
Using PyPDFLoader from langchain_community with default settings on a 10-page PDF, what do you usually get from load()?
One Document per page, with the page number in metadata
One Document for the whole file with no page info
One Document per paragraph found in the text
One Document per 1,000 characters of text
By default PyPDFLoader creates a Document for each page and records the page in metadata. Chunking is done later by a splitter.
In legacy LangChain memory, what does ConversationBufferWindowMemory(k=3) keep in the prompt?
Only the last 3 exchanges of the conversation
Only the first 3 exchanges of the conversation
A summary limited to 3 sentences of the chat
The 3 past messages most similar to the query
The window buffer keeps a sliding window of the most recent k interactions, so older turns drop out.
In LCEL based LangChain, which wrapper adds per-session chat history to any runnable, using a session id from the config?
RunnableWithMessageHistory
RunnableWithMemoryBuffer
ConversationSessionRunnable
RunnableHistoryParallel
RunnableWithMessageHistory loads and saves messages for the session_id passed in config, replacing the older memory classes.
LLMChain is deprecated in recent LangChain releases. What is the recommended replacement for a chain that formats a prompt and calls a model?
Composing prompt | model with LCEL
Subclassing LLMChain and overriding run()
Calling model.predict() with a template
Wrapping the prompt in a SequentialChain
LangChain now recommends LCEL composition; prompt | model (often | parser) does what LLMChain did, with streaming and batching for free.
In current LangChain, which separate package do you install to use the ChatOpenAI integration?
langchain-openai
langchain-core
langchain-text-splitters
langchain-experimental
Major providers ship as partner packages such as langchain-openai and langchain-anthropic. langchain-core holds base abstractions only.
What happens when you invoke chain = model_a.with_fallbacks([model_b])?
model_b is called only if model_a raises an error
Both models run and the faster answer is kept
model_b is called when model_a's answer is short
The two models alternate on successive calls
with_fallbacks catches exceptions from the primary runnable (for example rate limits) and retries with the fallbacks in order.
llamaindex: In LlamaIndex, what does VectorStoreIndex.from_documents(documents) do by default?
Splits documents into nodes, embeds them and stores the vectors
Stores the raw documents and embeds them only at query time
Builds a keyword table from the documents without embeddings
Summarizes every document with the LLM and stores the summaries
from_documents runs node parsing and embedding up front, so queries can do a fast top-k similarity search.
How does a SummaryIndex (formerly ListIndex) in LlamaIndex differ from a VectorStoreIndex at query time by default?
It sends all nodes to the LLM instead of top-k similar ones
It retrieves only the single most similar node
It ranks nodes with BM25 instead of embeddings
It answers from cached summaries without an LLM
A SummaryIndex keeps nodes in a list and by default iterates over all of them, which suits whole-document summarization.
Which LlamaIndex index type is the best fit when you want to summarize an entire short document, not answer a narrow factual question?
SummaryIndex
VectorStoreIndex
KeywordTableIndex
PropertyGraphIndex
Summarization needs every chunk, and SummaryIndex passes all nodes to the LLM. Vector search would return only a few chunks.
What is the simplest LlamaIndex call to turn an existing index into an object that answers natural-language questions?
index.as_query_engine()
index.as_vector_store()
index.to_retriever_pipeline()
index.build_answerer()
as_query_engine() wraps a retriever and a response synthesizer; you then call query_engine.query("...").
In LlamaIndex, what is the main difference between a retriever and a query engine?
A retriever returns nodes; a query engine also synthesizes an answer
A retriever calls the LLM; a query engine only does vector search
A retriever works on files; a query engine works on databases
A retriever is async only; a query engine is sync only
Retrievers fetch relevant nodes (NodeWithScore). A query engine combines retrieval with response synthesis by the LLM.
What does index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=5).retrieve("What is RAG?") return in LlamaIndex?
A list of up to 5 NodeWithScore objects
A single string answer written by the LLM
The 5 original Document objects, unscored
A Response object with source_nodes only
Retrievers return scored nodes. Only a query engine or chat engine produces a generated Response.
A LlamaIndex query engine retrieves several chunks that do not all fit in one LLM call. Which response_mode makes one call per chunk, improving the answer step by step?
refine
compact
tree_summarize
no_text
refine sends the first chunk, then asks the LLM to refine the answer with each next chunk. compact first packs chunks to reduce calls.
In LlamaIndex, which response_mode returns only the retrieved nodes, without asking the LLM to write an answer?
no_text
refine
accumulate
simple_summarize
With no_text the query engine runs retrieval only; the nodes are available in response.source_nodes.
Your LlamaIndex RAG app returns weakly related chunks. Which node postprocessor drops retrieved nodes whose score is below a threshold?
SimilarityPostprocessor(similarity_cutoff=0.75)
SentenceSplitter(chunk_size=0.75)
MetadataReplacementPostProcessor(0.75)
TitleExtractor(threshold=0.75)
SimilarityPostprocessor filters NodeWithScore results by similarity_cutoff before synthesis.
Which LlamaIndex node parser splits text into chunks while trying to keep sentences whole, using chunk_size and chunk_overlap?
SentenceSplitter
MarkdownNodeParser
HierarchicalNodeParser
SummaryExtractor
SentenceSplitter is the default text splitter: it respects sentence boundaries within the configured token budget.
Which LlamaIndex node parser uses embedding similarity between neighboring sentences to choose chunk boundaries?
SemanticSplitterNodeParser
TokenTextSplitter
SentenceWindowNodeParser
CodeSplitter
The semantic splitter places breakpoints where adjacent sentence embeddings differ most, instead of using a fixed size.
In LlamaIndex, what does SentenceWindowNodeParser store in each node's metadata to help answer quality?
The surrounding sentences around that sentence
The embedding vector of the whole document
A list of questions the sentence answers
The token count of the parent document
Each node is one sentence, and the window of nearby sentences is kept in metadata so a postprocessor can swap it in before synthesis.
You want each LlamaIndex node to carry a list of questions it can answer, to improve retrieval. Which metadata extractor fits?
QuestionsAnsweredExtractor
TitleExtractor
KeywordExtractor
SummaryExtractor
QuestionsAnsweredExtractor asks the LLM for questions each node answers and stores them in node metadata.
How are metadata extractors such as TitleExtractor and KeywordExtractor usually applied in LlamaIndex?
As transformations in an IngestionPipeline
As arguments to query_engine.query()
As response modes of the synthesizer
As retrievers inside a RouterQueryEngine
Extractors are transformations: IngestionPipeline(transformations=[SentenceSplitter(), TitleExtractor(), ...]) runs them on nodes.
A LlamaIndex node has a file_path metadata key that should help the LLM but not affect embeddings. Which node setting controls this?
excluded_embed_metadata_keys
excluded_llm_metadata_keys
metadata_template
text_template
Keys in excluded_embed_metadata_keys are hidden from the embedding model but still shown to the LLM, unless also excluded there.
How do you save a LlamaIndex index to disk so it can be reloaded later without re-embedding?
index.storage_context.persist(persist_dir="./storage")
index.save_vectors(path="./storage")
Settings.persist(index, dir="./storage")
index.dump(persist_dir="./storage")
The StorageContext holds the docstore, index store and vector store; persist() writes them to persist_dir.
After persisting a LlamaIndex index to ./storage, which code reloads it?
load_index_from_storage(StorageContext.from_defaults(persist_dir="./storage"))
VectorStoreIndex.from_documents("./storage")
StorageContext.load_index("./storage", rebuild=True)
Settings.load(persist_dir="./storage")
You rebuild the StorageContext from the persist directory and pass it to load_index_from_storage.
Which stores does a default LlamaIndex StorageContext group together?
Document store, index store and vector store
Prompt store, model store and cache store
Session store, user store and token store
File store, image store and audio store
StorageContext bundles the docstore (nodes), the index store (index metadata) and the vector store, plus an optional graph store.
In LlamaIndex 0.10 and later, what replaces the deprecated ServiceContext for setting the global LLM and embedding model?
The Settings object, for example Settings.llm
A StorageContext passed to every index
Environment variables read by each node
A ServiceRegistry singleton per index
Settings holds global defaults such as llm, embed_model and chunk_size; you can still pass components locally to override them.
You have separate LlamaIndex query engines for HR policies and for engineering docs. Which component chooses between them per question using LLM selection?
RouterQueryEngine
SubQuestionQueryEngine
RetrieverQueryEngine
TransformQueryEngine
RouterQueryEngine uses a selector to pick the best query engine from their descriptions. SubQuestionQueryEngine splits one question into parts.
langgraph: In LangGraph, what must you call on a StateGraph before you can invoke it?
compile()
build()
start()
freeze()
graph.compile() validates the graph and returns a runnable CompiledGraph that supports invoke and stream.
In a LangGraph StateGraph, what should a node function return?
A dict with updates to some state keys
The name of the next node as a string
A full copy of the graph definition
Nothing, it must mutate state in place
Nodes return partial state updates; LangGraph merges them into the state using each key's reducer.
A LangGraph state is defined as class State(TypedDict): items: Annotated[list, operator.add]. Two nodes return {"items": [1]} and {"items": [2]}. What happens to items?
The lists are concatenated
The last update overwrites the list
An error is raised for a duplicate key
Only the first update is kept
Annotated with operator.add sets a reducer, so updates are appended. Without a reducer, a new value overwrites the old one.
Which LangGraph reducer is used for a messages key so that new messages are appended and messages with an existing id are replaced?
add_messages
operator.add
merge_dicts
append_unique
add_messages appends new messages and updates existing ones by id. MessagesState uses it for its messages key.
In LangGraph, what are START and END?
Special node names marking the graph entry and exit
Methods that run and stop a compiled graph
Reducers that reset the state at each run
Checkpointers for the first and last step
graph.add_edge(START, "first") sets the entry point; routing to END finishes the run.
What does graph.add_edge("a", "b") mean in a LangGraph StateGraph?
After node a finishes, node b always runs next
Node b runs only if node a raises an error
Nodes a and b share the same function
Node a may call node b as a tool
A normal edge is unconditional. Use add_conditional_edges when the next step depends on the state.
In LangGraph, add_conditional_edges("agent", route, {"tools": "tools", "done": END}). What must route return?
A key of the mapping, such as "tools" or "done"
A boolean that enables or disables the edge
The full updated state for the next node
A numeric index into the list of nodes
The routing function inspects the state and returns a value; the path map translates it into the destination node.
In a typical LangGraph ReAct agent, what does the prebuilt tools_condition routing function do?
Routes to the tools node if the last message has tool calls
Routes to the tools node on every second iteration
Routes to END if any tool raised an exception
Routes to the tool with the highest confidence
tools_condition checks the last AI message: tool calls send the flow to the ToolNode, otherwise the graph ends.
A LangGraph run fails with GraphRecursionError. What is the most likely cause?
A cycle ran more supersteps than the recursion limit
A node imported a module recursively
The state contained a nested dictionary
Two nodes were given the same reducer
LangGraph stops runs that exceed recursion_limit steps. Fix the loop exit condition, or raise the limit in the config if the loop is intended.
To pause a LangGraph graph for human approval and resume it later, what must the graph be compiled with?
A checkpointer, such as InMemorySaver
A larger recursion_limit value
The debug=True compile flag
A reducer on every state key
Interrupts save the state to a checkpoint so execution can resume; without a checkpointer there is nowhere to persist it.
Inside a LangGraph node you call value = interrupt({"question": "Approve?"}). How do you resume and supply the human answer?
Invoke again with Command(resume=answer) and the same thread_id
Call graph.resume(answer) with no config at all
Edit the node code and restart the run from START
Send the answer as a new user message in a new thread
interrupt() pauses the run; invoking with Command(resume=...) on the same thread makes interrupt return that value.
Which LangGraph compile option pauses execution before a given node runs, for example to review a planned tool call?
interrupt_before=["tools"]
checkpoint_before=["tools"]
pause_on=["tools"]
breakpoints=["tools"]
compile(checkpointer=..., interrupt_before=[...]) sets static breakpoints; interrupt_after works the same way after a node.
When a LangGraph graph has a checkpointer, which config value separates the saved state of different conversations?
configurable.thread_id
configurable.run_name
metadata.user_id
recursion_limit
Checkpoints are stored per thread. Invoking with {"configurable": {"thread_id": "42"}} continues that thread's state.
Which checkpointer is suited to quick local experiments in LangGraph but loses all state when the process exits?
InMemorySaver (MemorySaver)
PostgresSaver
SqliteSaver
RedisSaver
The in-memory saver keeps checkpoints in a Python dict; use a database-backed saver such as Postgres for production.
With a LangGraph checkpointer, which method lets you inspect earlier checkpoints of a thread to replay or fork from them (time travel)?
graph.get_state_history(config)
graph.list_threads(config)
graph.rollback(config)
graph.get_node_logs(config)
get_state_history yields past StateSnapshots; invoking with a checkpoint's config resumes or forks from that point.
A human reviewer wants to correct a value in a paused LangGraph thread before it resumes. Which method writes that change?
graph.update_state(config, values)
graph.patch_node(config, values)
graph.set_checkpoint(values)
graph.reset(config, values)
update_state applies an update to the thread's current state as if a node had produced it, using the same reducers.
In LangGraph, how can a node both update the state and decide which node runs next, for example to hand off to another agent?
Return Command(update={...}, goto="agent_b")
Return the string "agent_b" from the node
Raise a HandoffException("agent_b")
Call graph.add_edge inside the node
Command combines a state update with dynamic routing, which is the usual way to implement agent handoffs.
A LangGraph workflow must run the same summarize node once per document, where the number of documents is known only at run time. Which feature fits?
Returning Send objects from a conditional edge
Adding one static edge per possible document
Raising recursion_limit to the document count
Giving the node an operator.add reducer only
Send("summarize", {"doc": d}) fans out dynamic parallel tasks (map-reduce); a reducer then collects the results.
In a LangGraph supervisor multi-agent design, what does the supervisor do?
Decides which worker agent acts next
Stores checkpoints for all the workers
Executes Python code that workers write
Merges state keys with custom reducers
The supervisor is an LLM node that routes the task to specialized agents and decides when the work is finished.
How can a compiled LangGraph graph be reused inside another LangGraph graph?
Add the compiled graph as a node in the parent
Merge both graphs with the | operator
Copy its edges into the parent's reducer
Pass it to the parent as a checkpointer
Subgraphs are added with add_node like any node; they share state keys with the parent or are wrapped in a function that maps state.
dspy: In DSPy, what does the signature string "question -> answer" declare?
One input field named question and one output field answer
A prompt template with the literal words question and answer
A function that maps answers back to their questions
A training example with a question and its gold answer
A signature declares typed input and output fields. DSPy builds the actual prompt from it.
In a class-based DSPy signature, what is the docstring of the class used for?
As the task instructions for the language model
As a comment ignored at run time
As the name of the output field
As the metric to optimize against
The docstring becomes the instruction; dspy.InputField and dspy.OutputField declare the fields.
Which DSPy signature declares two inputs and one output?
"context, question -> answer"
"context -> question, answer"
"context | question => answer"
"answer <- context + question"
Inputs are comma separated on the left of the arrow and outputs on the right.
What is the difference between dspy.Predict and dspy.ChainOfThought for the same signature?
ChainOfThought adds a reasoning output before the answer
ChainOfThought runs several models and votes
Predict adds a reasoning field, ChainOfThought does not
Predict is only for classification signatures
ChainOfThought extends the signature with a reasoning field, so the model reasons step by step before the outputs.
After qa = dspy.ChainOfThought("question -> answer") and pred = qa(question="..."), how do you read the answer?
pred.answer
pred["output"][0]
pred.completions.text
qa.answer
Predictions expose output fields as attributes named after the signature, so pred.answer (and pred.reasoning here).
Which DSPy module lets the model alternate reasoning steps with calls to tools you provide?
dspy.ReAct
dspy.Predict
dspy.Retrieve
dspy.Signature
dspy.ReAct(signature, tools=[...]) implements the Reason plus Act loop over the given tools.
How do you set the default language model for DSPy modules in DSPy 2.5 and later?
dspy.configure(lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-4o-mini"))
dspy.Predict.set_model("gpt-4o-mini")
os.environ["DSPY_MODEL"] = "gpt-4o-mini"
dspy.Signature(model="gpt-4o-mini")
dspy.configure sets global settings; dspy.LM uses provider/model strings (through LiteLLM).
What is a DSPy optimizer (formerly called a teleprompter)?
An algorithm that tunes a program's prompts or weights for a metric
A module that rewrites user questions before retrieval
A tool that counts and reduces prompt tokens
A server that hosts compiled DSPy programs
Optimizers such as BootstrapFewShot and MIPROv2 use a training set and a metric to improve demos, instructions or weights.
What does the DSPy optimizer BootstrapFewShot primarily produce?
Few-shot demos created by running the program on training data
Fine-tuned model weights from the training set
A rewritten signature with new field names
A new retrieval index built from the trainset
It runs a teacher program on training examples, keeps traces that pass the metric, and inserts them as demonstrations.
Which DSPy optimizer jointly searches over instructions and few-shot examples, using Bayesian optimization?
MIPROv2
LabeledFewShot
BootstrapFewShot
KNNFewShot
MIPROv2 proposes candidate instructions and demos, then searches combinations against the metric.
You have labeled examples but no time for bootstrapping. Which DSPy optimizer simply inserts k of your labeled examples as demos?
LabeledFewShot
MIPROv2
BootstrapFinetune
COPRO
LabeledFewShot(k=...) samples labeled training examples directly as demonstrations without running the program.
How do you run a DSPy optimizer on a program?
optimizer.compile(program, trainset=trainset)
program.fit(optimizer, trainset)
dspy.optimize(program).run(trainset)
optimizer.train(program, epochs=3)
compile returns a new, optimized copy of the program; the original program is unchanged.
In DSPy, what does "compiling" a program mean?
Optimizing its prompts or weights against a metric
Translating the Python code into C for speed
Checking that all signatures have valid types
Bundling the program into one prompt string
Compiling uses an optimizer, training data and a metric to produce better demos, instructions or fine-tuned weights.
How do you save an optimized DSPy program and load it back later?
program.save("p.json") then program.load("p.json")
dspy.export(program) then dspy.import("p")
pickle the LM, then rebuild the signatures
optimizer.save() then optimizer.restore()
save writes the learned state (demos, instructions) to a file; load restores it into a program with the same structure.
In DSPy, how do you compose several modules into one program?
Subclass dspy.Module and call the modules in forward()
Chain them with the | operator into a Pipeline
List them in a YAML file passed to dspy.compile
Merge their signatures into a single string
A dspy.Module declares submodules in __init__ and wires them together in forward(), like a PyTorch module.
Why should submodules of a DSPy program be assigned as attributes in __init__ (for example self.generate = dspy.ChainOfThought(...))?
So optimizers can find and tune their predictors
So they run in parallel threads automatically
So DSPy can cache their API keys
So they are excluded from compilation
Optimizers discover predictors via named_predictors() on the module tree, which comes from these attributes.
What is the usual signature of a DSPy metric function?
metric(example, pred, trace=None)
metric(pred) -> str
metric(trainset, devset)
metric(lm, prompt, temperature)
The metric compares the gold example with the prediction; trace is set during optimization so metrics can be stricter there.
A DSPy metric returns a float score during evaluation but a bool when trace is not None. Why is this pattern common?
Bootstrapping needs a pass or fail decision to keep demos
Evaluate cannot handle float metrics at all
trace is None only when the LM call failed
Booleans make the LM calls run faster
During compilation the trace is present and the optimizer keeps only demos that pass, so a strict boolean works best.
How do you mark which fields of a dspy.Example are inputs, so the rest are treated as labels?
Example(question=q, answer=a).with_inputs("question")
Example(inputs=["question"], answer=a)
Example(question=q).labels("answer")
Example(q, a).set_input_index(0)
with_inputs names the input keys; other fields are labels that the metric can compare against.
Which DSPy utility scores a program on a dev set with a metric, optionally using several threads?
dspy.Evaluate(devset=devset, metric=metric)
dspy.Predict(devset, metric)
dspy.Signature.score(devset)
dspy.LM.benchmark(devset)
Evaluate runs the program on every example and reports the aggregate metric; num_threads parallelizes calls.
crewai: Which three attributes give a CrewAI Agent its persona?
role, goal and backstory
name, task and prompt
title, mission and history
persona, objective and context
Every CrewAI Agent is defined by role, goal and backstory; these shape the system prompt the agent works with.
What is the purpose of the backstory attribute of a CrewAI Agent?
It gives context that shapes the agent's style and choices
It stores the agent's past task results across runs
It lists the tools the agent is allowed to call
It sets the order in which agents take turns
The backstory is persona text added to the prompt, for example years of experience or domain focus. Memory stores past results, not backstory.
Which two fields must you provide when creating a CrewAI Task?
description and expected_output
description and output_file
name and prompt
goal and tools
A Task needs a description of the work and an expected_output that tells the agent what a finished result looks like.
In CrewAI, how do you make task_c explicitly receive the outputs of task_a and task_b?
Task(..., context=[task_a, task_b])
Task(..., inputs=[task_a, task_b])
Task(..., depends_on=[task_a, task_b])
Task(..., previous=[task_a, task_b])
The context parameter lists tasks whose outputs are passed to this task as context.
A CrewAI task description contains {topic}. What fills it in?
crew.kickoff(inputs={"topic": "AI"})
Task.format(topic="AI")
Agent(variables={"topic": "AI"})
Crew(template_vars={"topic": "AI"})
kickoff interpolates the inputs dict into placeholders in agent and task fields before the crew runs.
What happens to tasks in a CrewAI crew that uses Process.sequential?
They run in list order, each seeing earlier outputs as context
They all run at once and the results are merged
A manager agent picks their order at run time
They run in random order to avoid bias
In a sequential process tasks execute one after another, and the output of a task is available as context to the next.
What must you add when you set a CrewAI Crew to process=Process.hierarchical?
A manager_llm or a manager_agent
A context list on every task
A memory=True flag on the crew
An output_file on the last task
The hierarchical process needs a manager that plans, delegates tasks to agents and validates results.
In a hierarchical CrewAI process, who decides which agent works on each task?
The manager, which delegates and reviews the work
The first agent in the agents list
The task with the shortest description
Each agent votes on the assignments
The manager agent (or one created from manager_llm) coordinates the crew instead of a fixed order.
How do you turn a plain Python function into a CrewAI tool most simply?
Decorate it with @tool("Tool name") from crewai.tools
Decorate it with @crew_tool from crewai.agents
Pass it to Agent(functions=[...]) unchanged
Register it with Crew.add_tool(func) at kickoff

execute
run_tool
__call__

Run its tasks at the same time as other agents

Only a buffer of the last ten messages
Only a vector store of uploaded files
Episodic, procedural and sensory memory

Lessons and results that persist across separate crew runs
The exact prompt text of the current task only

The API keys used by each agent's model

A list of strings, one per agent in the crew
Nothing, the result is only written to output files
The final agent object with its updated memory

The agent asks a person for feedback before finalizing the answer
The task description must be typed in at run time
The task is skipped unless a person approves it first
The task output is written to the terminal only

autogen: In AutoGen 0.2, what is ConversableAgent?
The base agent class that sends, receives and replies to messages
A wrapper that turns any API into a single tool
The manager that picks speakers in group chats
A sandbox that executes generated Python code

user_proxy.initiate_chat(assistant, message="...")
assistant.start(user_proxy, prompt="...")
autogen.run_chat(user_proxy, assistant, "...")
user_proxy.send_task(assistant, task="...")

It replies automatically and never prompts a person
It only accepts input typed by a person
It asks a person before each code run
It refuses to answer messages from humans

In AutoGen 0.2, when does an agent with human_input_mode="TERMINATE" ask a person for input?
Only when a termination condition is met
Before every single reply it sends
Only when its code execution fails
Never, the mode disables human input

"ALWAYS"
"NEVER"
"TERMINATE"
"AUTO"

In AutoGen 0.2, what does a UserProxyAgent do by default when it receives a message with a Python code block?
Executes the code and replies with the output
Sends the code to an LLM to review it
Saves the code without running it
Forwards the code to the group chat manager

In AutoGen 0.2, what does code_execution_config={"work_dir": "coding", "use_docker": True} do?
Runs code in a Docker container, with files in coding
Saves generated code to coding without running it
Runs code on the host and logs to Docker
Installs Docker inside the coding directory

Why is running LLM-generated code in Docker recommended in AutoGen?
It isolates untrusted code from the host machine
It makes the LLM write shorter code blocks
It is needed for agents to read code output
It removes the need for termination conditions
Generated code can delete files or install packages; a container limits the damage to the host.

Set code_execution_config=False
Set human_input_mode="NEVER"
Set llm_config=False
Set max_consecutive_auto_reply=0

In AutoGen 0.4 and later, which executor runs code blocks inside a container instead of on the host?
DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor
LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor
JupyterCodeExecutor
PythonReplExecutor
DockerCommandLineCodeExecutor runs each block in a Docker container; LocalCommandLineCodeExecutor runs on the host.
In AutoGen 0.2, what is the role of GroupChatManager in a group chat?
Picks the next speaker and relays messages to the agents
Executes all code that the agents write
Stores conversation history in a database
Merges every agent into one large prompt
The manager wraps a GroupChat, selects who speaks next and broadcasts each message to the participants.
In AutoGen 0.2 GroupChat, what does speaker_selection_method="round_robin" do?
Agents speak in a fixed rotating order
An LLM picks the most suitable next speaker
A random agent is chosen each round
A person picks the next speaker each turn

What does max_round limit in an AutoGen 0.2 GroupChat?
The maximum number of rounds before the chat stops
How many agents may join the group chat
How many code blocks each agent may run
How many tokens one agent message may use
max_round is a safety stop for the group conversation.
In AutoGen 0.4 AgentChat, how does SelectorGroupChat differ from RoundRobinGroupChat?
It uses a model to choose the next speaker
It lets only one agent speak in each run
It runs every agent in parallel on one task
It requires a human to choose each speaker

In AutoGen 0.2, an agent has is_termination_msg=lambda m: "TERMINATE" in (m.get("content") or ""). When does the chat end?
When the agent receives a message containing TERMINATE
When the agent itself sends its first reply
After TERMINATE appears in any system prompt
When the message has no content field

Retries a failed LLM call up to three times
Limits group chats to three participants
Keeps only the last three messages in history

Stops when either condition is met
Stops only when both conditions are met
Raises an error, conditions cannot combine
Applies the second condition after a restart

The final message string only
A new team object with updated memory
A list of code files written by agents

In AutoGen 0.2, what does register_function(f, caller=assistant, executor=user_proxy) set up?

The user proxy proposes calls and the assistant runs them
Both agents run f in parallel on each message

The number of turns in that conversation
The number of agents allowed to speak
The number of retries per LLM call
The number of tools each agent can use

semantic-kernel: What is a plugin in Semantic Kernel?
A named group of functions the kernel exposes to AI
A model provider such as OpenAI or Azure
A vector database used to store embeddings
A prompt template file for a single request
Plugins group related functions (native code or prompts) that the kernel and the model can call.
In Semantic Kernel for Python, which decorator exposes a class method as a kernel function?
@kernel_function
@sk_plugin
@semantic_function
@native_tool
@kernel_function (from semantic_kernel.functions) marks a method; an optional description helps the model choose it.
In Semantic Kernel for C#, which attribute marks a method as callable by the kernel?
[KernelFunction]
[SKPlugin]
[AIFunction]
[PromptFunction]
[KernelFunction] exposes the method; [Description] adds text the model uses for function calling.
In Semantic Kernel, what is the main difference between a native function and a semantic (prompt) function?
Native functions are code; semantic ones are prompts sent to an LLM
Native functions call an LLM; semantic ones run locally
Native functions are C# only; semantic ones Python only
Native functions are sync; semantic ones are only async
Native functions run your C#, Python or Java code. Semantic functions render a prompt template and call a model.
Which task fits a native function better than a semantic function in Semantic Kernel?

Summarizing a long customer email
Rewriting text in a friendlier tone
Translating a paragraph to Korean

{{$city}}
{city}
${city}
<<city>>

In older Semantic Kernel prompt plugins stored on disk, which two files define each prompt function?

prompt.yaml and schema.xml
function.md and settings.ini
template.txt and model.toml

PromptVariables
FunctionContext
PluginInputs

Running the Handlebars template engine twice
Calling every plugin and letting the model choose

The ChatHistory class
Prompt template variables
Kernel filters

assistant
tool

Requests authenticate with x-api-key and pin the API version with anthropic-version (for example 2023-06-01).
Which parameter is required in every Anthropic Messages API request, along with model and messages?
max_tokens
temperature
system
stop_sequences
max_tokens is required and caps the number of tokens Claude may generate.
Where does Claude's reply text appear in a Messages API response?
In content, a list of blocks such as type text
In choices[0].message.content
In a top-level completion string
In output.text of the first candidate
The response content is a list of typed blocks, so text sits in content[i].text where type is text.
A Messages API response has stop_reason "max_tokens". What should you do if you need the full answer?
Raise max_tokens and send the request again
Lower temperature so the model writes less
Remove the system prompt and send it again
Nothing, max_tokens means it finished
"max_tokens" means generation was cut off; "end_turn" is a natural finish.
How do you pass a system prompt in the Anthropic Messages API?
In the top-level system parameter
As a message with role system
In the anthropic-system header
As the first assistant message
Unlike some other APIs, messages only use user and assistant roles; system instructions go in system.
Which kind of content best belongs in a Claude system prompt?
A role, rules and context that apply to the whole chat
The user's latest question for this turn
Tool results returned by your code
The final answer you expect Claude to copy
System prompts set persistent behavior; per-turn questions and tool results go in the messages.
You give Claude tools in the Messages API and it decides to use one. What is the response's stop_reason?
"tool_use"
"function_call"
"tool_calls"
"end_turn"
The response contains tool_use blocks and stop_reason "tool_use", signaling your code should run the tool.
How do you return a tool's output to Claude in the Messages API?
A user message with a tool_result block and the tool_use_id
An assistant message with the result as text
A message with role tool and the call id
A system parameter update with the result
tool_result blocks go in the next user message and reference the id of the matching tool_use block.
How do you describe a tool's input parameters to Claude in the Messages API?
With a JSON Schema in the tool's input_schema
With a Python type hint string in name
With an OpenAPI URL in description
With an example call in the system prompt
Each tool has name, description and input_schema; Claude's tool_use input follows that schema.
Which tool_choice setting makes Claude call one specific tool named get_weather?
{"type": "tool", "name": "get_weather"}
{"type": "auto", "name": "get_weather"}
{"type": "any", "tool": "get_weather"}
{"force": "get_weather"}
"auto" lets Claude decide, "any" forces some tool, "tool" forces the named one and "none" disables tools.
How do you mark the end of a reusable prompt prefix for prompt caching in the Anthropic API?
Add cache_control {"type": "ephemeral"} to a content block
Send the header x-cache-prefix: true
Set cache=true at the top of the request
Wrap the prefix in <cache> tags in the text
cache_control on a block caches everything up to and including that block for later requests.
Which usage field shows that a Messages API request was served from the prompt cache?
cache_read_input_tokens
cached_output_tokens
prompt_cache_hits
reused_prompt_tokens
cache_read_input_tokens counts tokens read from cache; cache_creation_input_tokens counts tokens written to it.
You cache a long system prompt with Anthropic prompt caching, then change one word at its start. What happens on the next request?
The cache misses, because the prefix must match exactly
The cache hits, since most of the text is unchanged
The request fails with a cache conflict error
Only the changed word is sent to the model
Caching matches an exact prefix (tools, then system, then messages); any change before a breakpoint invalidates it.
What is the default lifetime of an Anthropic prompt cache entry, refreshed each time it is used?
5 minutes
24 hours
30 seconds
7 days
The default ephemeral cache lives about 5 minutes and is refreshed on each hit; a longer 1-hour option also exists.
How do you send an image to Claude in the Messages API?
An image content block with a base64 or URL source
An image_url string inside a text block
A multipart file upload to /v1/images
A link to the image in the system prompt
Image blocks use source types such as base64 (with media_type) or url, placed in user message content.
Which image formats does the Claude Messages API accept as image inputs?
JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP
JPEG, PNG, BMP and TIFF
PNG, SVG, HEIC and WebP
JPEG, PSD, GIF and RAW
The supported media types are image/jpeg, image/png, image/gif and image/webp.
You ask Claude to compare two photos. How should the request be structured?
One user message with two image blocks and a text block
Two requests, then merge both answers yourself
Both images in the system parameter as text
One image per assistant message in the history
A single message can hold several image blocks plus text, so Claude sees both images together.
Which Anthropic API endpoint returns the input token count of a request without generating a response?
POST /v1/messages/count_tokens
GET /v1/tokens
POST /v1/messages?dry_run=true
POST /v1/tokenize
The token counting endpoint accepts the same model, system, tools and messages and returns input_tokens.
You set max_tokens to 50 for a task that needs a long answer. What is the likely result?
A truncated answer with stop_reason "max_tokens"
An API error saying the limit is too small
A full answer with extra tokens billed
Claude summarizes to fit in exactly 50 tokens
max_tokens is a hard cap; the model is not told to be brief, so the output just stops at the limit.
gemini-api: In the Gemini API REST interface, which method generates a response for a model?
models/{model}:generateContent
models/{model}:complete
chat/completions
models/{model}:predictText
generateContent returns a full response; streamGenerateContent returns it in chunks.
In a Gemini generateContent request, which role names are used in contents for a chat history?
user and model
user and assistant
human and ai
client and bot
Gemini uses role "model" for its own turns, not "assistant".
In the Gemini API, what is a content's parts field?
A list of pieces such as text, inline data or function calls
The list of safety ratings for the response
The token counts of each section of a prompt
The ordered list of model versions to try
A content holds a role plus parts; one turn can mix text and media parts.
Using the google-genai Python SDK, how do you read the text of a response?
response.text
response.choices[0].text
response.content[0].text
response.output_text[0]
response.text is a shortcut to the text parts of the first candidate.
In the Gemini API, how do you give the model persistent instructions such as a persona?
The system_instruction field of the request or config
A content with role system in contents
A header named x-goog-system-prompt
A safety setting with the instruction text
system_instruction is separate from contents; contents only use the user and model roles.
In the google-genai Python SDK, where do you set a system instruction for generate_content?
config=types.GenerateContentConfig(system_instruction=...)
client.models.system = "..." before the call
contents=[{"role": "system", "text": "..."}]
genai.configure(system_prompt="...")
Generation options such as system_instruction, temperature and tools go in GenerateContentConfig.
How do you declare a function the Gemini model may call?
In tools, as function_declarations with a JSON Schema
As a Python string in the system instruction
In safety_settings with the function name
As a URL in the generation config
Each declaration has a name, description and parameters schema; the model replies with a functionCall part.
After the Gemini model returns a functionCall part, how do you send your function's result back?
A functionResponse part in the next request
A new system_instruction with the result
A model role message containing only text
The result in generationConfig.output
You append the model's functionCall turn and then a functionResponse part with the name and result.
Which Gemini function calling mode forces the model to always return a function call?
ANY
AUTO
NONE
REQUIRED
function_calling_config mode ANY forces a call (optionally limited by allowed_function_names); AUTO lets the model choose.
In the google-genai Python SDK, what happens when you pass a Python function directly in tools?
The SDK can call it automatically and return the final answer
The SDK sends the function's source code as text
The request fails until you write a JSON schema
The function runs once before the request is sent
Automatic function calling builds the declaration from the signature and docstring, runs the function and continues.
How do you send a small image inline with a Gemini prompt over REST?
An inline_data part with mime_type and base64 data
An image_url part with a public link only
A multipart upload in the same HTTP request
A text part containing the file path
Inline data suits small files; larger ones should be uploaded with the Files API first.
You need Gemini to analyze a large video file that would make the request too big to send inline. What should you use?
Upload it with the Files API and reference the file
Split the video into many inline_data parts
Convert the video to text and send that instead
Send a YouTube search query in the prompt
The Files API stores media temporarily and you pass the file reference in a part.
Which kinds of input can Gemini 1.5 and later models accept in one prompt?
Text, images, audio and video
Text and images only
Text and audio only
Text, images and 3D meshes
Gemini models are natively multimodal and accept audio and video in addition to text and images.
How can you check how many tokens a Gemini prompt uses before sending it to generateContent?
Call the countTokens method
Read the usage header from a HEAD request
Divide the character count by ten
Call generateContent with max tokens 0
countTokens returns the total tokens for the same contents, including media.
Gemini 1.5 Pro supports a very long context window. What does this most directly allow?
Putting whole books or long videos in a single prompt
Generating output of unlimited length
Remembering chats across separate API calls
Training the model on your private data
A large context window is about input size. Output length is limited separately and calls stay stateless.
You send the same large document to Gemini in many requests. Which feature can reduce cost for the repeated part?
Context caching
Grounding with Google Search
Function calling in ANY mode
Lowering the temperature
Context caching stores reusable input tokens so later requests can reference them at a lower rate.
Which tool lets Gemini 2.0 and later models base answers on fresh web results?
The google_search tool (Grounding with Google Search)
The code_execution tool with a web URL
A function declaration named search
A system instruction that says browse
Adding google_search to tools lets the model search and cite web sources.
When a Gemini response is grounded with Google Search, where do you find the sources it used?
In the candidate's grounding_metadata
In response.text after the answer
In the safety_ratings field
In the usage_metadata field
grounding_metadata holds search queries, source chunks and supports linking text segments to sources.
How do you ask Gemini to return JSON that follows a schema?
Set response_mime_type to application/json and a response_schema
Add the word JSON to the system instruction only
Set temperature to 0 and max tokens to 1
Use the streamGenerateContent method
Structured output uses response_mime_type plus response_schema in the generation config.
A Gemini candidate has finish_reason MAX_TOKENS. What happened?
Output stopped at the max_output_tokens limit
The model completed its answer normally
The response was blocked for safety
The model requested a function call
MAX_TOKENS means the output was cut off; STOP is a natural finish and SAFETY means it was blocked.
